title: Standing to play and the sandwich anecdote
summary: The men tell how Metoyer would eat a sandwich between choruses. They talk about trumpeters who stand to play, including Bunk Johnson, and Metoyer's duets with Ernie.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: And you know what he used to do? I know him have a sandwich in his hand and play his chorus. When the siphon player would play, he'd bite his hand and chew it and then he still might have a mouth full and he'd play that horn. It's just like if you don't have, it's just nothing. Yeah. I seen him do it.
We were talking about one of our trombone friends the other day, he keeps a lot of tobacco. He used to play. Well, he'd play.
And Arthur would do it, never spit no food in his hand.

I know you've heard of it. Out on the lake shore there, he used to play several jobs with old man Dave Perkins. Oh yeah, it's a new band. Yeah, out on the lake. And I know he used to play a job with them and he would be standing up, just like to do
Bung Johnson used to like to stand up, not all the time, but quite often he'd stand up, usually especially when he'd take a solo and it wasn't just to show off.

I didn't know whether it was habitual with him or if it was just a system he had. Probably could breathe easier. Even in teaching me. He'd sit me down by the music stand up, and he'd stand up. When he'd get his horn and he'd say, we're going to play a duet, he'd be standing up, making me sit down, he'd stand up all the day.
When you played duets, did you both play the melody or did he play the harmony with you? Well we would switch.
He would play the melody and he'd play the harmony and he'd fight the verse and I'd call it.
